body:
From separate safety tests to an orbital mission

Safety tests examine particular functions; an uncrewed orbital mission examines how the spacecraft works as a connected system during an actual journey to orbit and back. ISRO's reported sequence before the first crewed flight is G1, G2 and G3, followed by the first crewed mission, generally called H1. G1 is intended as an experimental flight to test new technologies early. G2 and G3 are intended to test the configuration planned for the first crewed mission.

The planned G1 flight includes Vyommitra, a half-humanoid robot used as part of testing. Vyommitra is not an astronaut, and a flight carrying it is still uncrewed. The purpose is to obtain information about the spacecraft and its systems before exposing people to the risks of flight.

Training and responsibility

The Human Space Flight Centre (HSFC) leads ISRO's human-spaceflight work. Astronaut preparation includes learning spacecraft procedures, practising in simulators, physical and medical training, and practising what to do during emergencies and after landing. ISRO's Astronaut Training Facility is in Bengaluru. The initial Gaganyaan astronaut-designates were chosen from Indian Air Force test pilots, according to ISRO's selection criteria.

India-wide participation and a Gujarat link

Gaganyaan is an ISRO-led national programme, supported by other Indian organisations and industries. The Space Applications Centre (SAC), Ahmedabad, has developed spread-spectrum modems for the Gaganyaan crew communication system. Communication between a spacecraft and ground teams is essential to monitor the crew and vehicle and pass instructions. Ahmedabad's role should not be confused with the launch site at Sriharikota or the astronaut training facility at Bengaluru.

Status and targets at the content cutoff

As of 4 November 2026, the verified programme reports treated G1 and the first crewed flight as planned, not accomplished. In a statement dated 6 August 2026, the Department of Space targeted G1 for the fourth quarter of 2026, with further uncrewed missions and a first crewed flight targeted by 2027. ISRO's 16 October 2026 update again described G1 as upcoming and targeted for 2026. These are planning dates, not confirmed launch dates or completed events.

Prelims focus

  • Planned pre-crew orbital sequence: G1, G2, G3, then H1.
  • G1: first planned uncrewed experimental orbital mission, with the half-humanoid Vyommitra.
  • Lead human-spaceflight centre: HSFC; astronaut training facility: Bengaluru.
  • Gujarat connection: SAC, Ahmedabad, developed modems for Gaganyaan crew communications.
  • Trap: A stated target date must not be described as a flight already completed.

[Sources: ISRO/Department of Space, Annual Report 2025–2026, section 2.6 'Gaganyaan', printed pp. 106–112; ISRO, Gaganyaan programme overview, section 'Crew training'; PIB/Department of Space, 'Key Milestones in Gaganyaan', 6 August 2026; ISRO, 'Crew Module–Service Module Separation Tests', 16 October 2026; PIB/Department of Space, 'Updates on the Space Applications Centre of ISRO', 3 April 2025; consulted 4 November 2026.]

title: Uncrewed Missions, Vyommitra and Preparation for the First Crew

body:
What a space station is

The Bharatiya Antariksh Station (BAS) is India's planned space station in low Earth orbit. A space station is an orbiting platform intended for longer-duration human stays and repeated scientific work. It differs from a short-duration spacecraft: the station is meant to remain in orbit as a facility, while visiting crews can travel to and from it in spacecraft.

The principal scientific advantage of an orbiting station is a sustained microgravity environment. Researchers can study, for example, how living organisms and materials behave when the usual effects of weight are greatly reduced. Such work has potential uses in life sciences, medicine and materials research.

How BAS connects to Gaganyaan

Gaganyaan's immediate goal is to demonstrate safe human launch, orbital flight and return. BAS extends India's ambitions towards longer-duration habitation and research. The programmes are linked because crew safety, life support, ground communication and orbital operations are essential for both. A space station also requires visiting spacecraft to approach and connect safely; this connection is called docking.

FeatureGaganyaan crewed missionBharatiya Antariksh Station
Main purposeDemonstrate a short human orbital flight and safe returnProvide an orbiting facility for longer stays and research
Main structureOrbital Module: Crew Module and Service ModulePlanned space station of 5 modules
At mission endCrew Module returns to EarthStation is intended to remain in orbit

Approved first module and longer-term target

The Union Cabinet approved the first BAS module, commonly designated BAS-01, under an expansion of the Gaganyaan programme in September 2024. The Government's published plan targets the first module by 2028 and a fully operational station of 5 modules by 2035. These are targets, not evidence that a station is already in operation. Official updates available by 4 November 2026 described design and development work, rather than a completed BAS launch.

At a glance, the short Gaganyaan crewed plan is for 3 astronauts to travel to about 400 km altitude for about 3 days on the HLVM3, live in an Orbital Module consisting of a Crew Module and Service Module, and return by sea splashdown. The planned uncrewed orbital missions G1, G2 and G3 precede the first crewed mission H1. BAS is a separate follow-on objective, with BAS-01 targeted for 2028 and the full station for 2035.

Do not interchange the names: Gaganyaan is the human spaceflight programme and its short-duration crewed spacecraft mission; BAS is the proposed longer-term orbital station. BAS-01 names the first planned station module, not Gaganyaan's returning Crew Module.

Prelims focus

  • BAS stands for Bharatiya Antariksh Station.
  • Planned location: low Earth orbit.
  • Approved first module: BAS-01, targeted by 2028.
  • Planned complete station: 5 modules, targeted for 2035.
  • Cabinet approval for the first module: September 2024.
  • Trap: BAS-01 and Gaganyaan's Crew Module are different spacecraft structures.

[Sources: PIB/Cabinet, 'Bharatiya Antariksh Station: Our own Space Station', 18 September 2024; PIB/Department of Space, 'Advantages and Benefits of Bharatiya Antariksh Station', 25 March 2026; PIB/Department of Space, 'Human Spaceflight and Indigenous Space Technology', 30 July 2026; ISRO, 'Indian Microgravity Experiments — IMEx-2026', 29 January 2026; consulted 4 November 2026.]

title: Bharatiya Antariksh Station: From Brief Flights to a Long-Term Orbital Platform
